title: Employees and Their Managers
description: Join a table to itself to show who reports to whom, keeping the head of the company.
statement:
Return every employee with the name of their manager: the columns `employee` and `manager`. The head of the company has no manager: show `NULL`.

Order by `employee`.
starter:
SELECT name AS employee
FROM employees;
variants: INSERT INTO employees VALUES (19, 'Aaron Adams', 1, 18, 50000, '2025-01-02'), (20, 'Zoe Zhang', NULL, NULL, 40000, '2025-01-03')
hints: The manager is also in `employees`. How can one table appear twice in `FROM`?
Give the two copies different aliases and join them on the manager's id.
Use a `LEFT JOIN` so that an employee with no manager is kept.
solution:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON m.id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.name;
explanation:
**The idea.** The manager is another row of the same table, found through `manager_id`. Join the table to **itself**, under two different aliases (`e` for the employee, `m` for the manager), and match `m.id = e.manager_id`. The join must be a `LEFT JOIN`, or the head of the company, whose `manager_id` is `NULL`, would disappear.

**Why aliases are needed.** Without `AS e` and `AS m` the two copies of `employees` would have the same name and every column reference would be ambiguous.

**Follow-up.** Chains of managers (who is the boss of my boss) need a *recursive* CTE: see the org chart problems.
